title: Real Casual Japanese
intro: Textbook Japanese is polite Japanese, and polite Japanese holds people at a distance. Casual speech is not sloppy です・ます — it has its own grammar: particles vanish, の and よね carry whole meanings, and a good half of what you say is reaction noise. The hard part is not producing it but knowing when you are allowed to, because switching down uninvited is presumptuous, while staying formal with a friend quietly tells them you do not consider them one. Start this from N4; the particle and 相槌 modules keep paying off all the way to N1.

stages.name: Switching down
stages.note: You already know plain form. What you are missing is the social rule for using it — read this before you make Japanese friends, not after.

stages.name: How it actually sounds
stages.note: The forms you learned, as they are really pronounced. Mostly a listening problem: you cannot catch 行かなきゃ if you only ever learned 行かなければ.

stages.name: The emotional layer
stages.note: Final particles and reactions. This is the stage that makes you sound like a person instead of a translation.

stages.name: Keeping the friendship
stages.note: Refusing and texting — the two places where casual Japanese can still cost you something.

modules.title: Dropping polite speech 敬語とタメ口
modules.blurb: Plain form between friends is called タメ口. Who may start it, and what it costs you to never start it.

items.ja: 敬語じゃなくていいよ。
items.r: けいごじゃなくていいよ。
items.en: You don't have to be formal with me.
items.note: This is an invitation, and it almost always comes from the older or more senior person. Wait for it rather than testing the water yourself.

タメ口 is plain-form speech between equals (タメ is gamblers' slang for a tie — the same roll of the dice — hence 'same age'). The offer is usually made once, lightly. If you politely decline it, you have chosen the distance.

items.ja: もう友達だし、普通に話していいよ。
items.r: もうともだちだし、ふつうにはなしていいよ。
items.en: We're friends now — talk to me normally.
items.note: 普通に話す is what Japanese people actually say for 'speak casually'. It is far more common in conversation than タメ口で話す.

items.ja: じゃあ、お言葉に甘えて。
items.r: じゃあ、おことばにあまえて。
items.en: Well then, I'll take you up on that.
items.note: The set reply to an offer you were hesitant to accept. It sounds slightly formal but is used between friends too — it shows you registered the offer as a kindness rather than just pocketing it.

items.en: Shall we drop the formal speech?
items.note: Only to someone your own age or younger, or someone you have genuinely become close to. Proposing this to a boss, a 先輩 or anyone clearly older is presumptuous no matter how friendly they have been.
Asking age early is normal among younger Japanese people precisely because the answer decides who speaks casually to whom. It is not the rude question it can be in English.

items.ja: 同い年だ！じゃあ敬語なしで話そう。
items.r: おないどしだ！じゃあけいごなしではなそう。
items.en: Same age! Let's drop the formal speech then.
items.note: Being the same age is the clearest licence there is. Once it is established, plain form is expected in both directions.

items.ja: 先輩・上司・お客さんには、ずっと敬語。
items.r: せんぱい・じょうし・おきゃくさんには、ずっとけいご。
items.en: With senpai, bosses and customers you stay polite — indefinitely.
items.note: Warmth is not permission. Someone can joke with you for years and still expect です・ます. A change in the relationship gets announced; it is never assumed.

items.ja: ずっと敬語だと、ちょっと距離を感じる。
items.r: ずっとけいごだと、ちょっときょりをかんじる。
items.en: If you stay in polite speech, it feels a bit distant.
items.note: The cost learners underestimate. With a friend your own age, です・ます is not the 'safe' option — it reads as holding them at arm's length, not as respect.

modules.title: Polite ⇄ casual 言い換え
modules.blurb: The same sentence in both registers. Converting on the fly is the actual skill — read the polite line, say the casual one.
modules.note: Casual is not just 'verb in plain form'. Three things happen at once: the です・ます ending drops, the particles disappear, and か is replaced by rising intonation. The particle drop is what your ear notices most.

items.note: Two changes at once: しています → してる, and を simply vanishes. Dropping particles is the single biggest thing that makes speech sound casual.
No か. A plain form with か attached (忙しいか？) sounds rough, or like an interrogation.
Do not put だ in. 何だ？ is a challenge, not a question.
わからない → わかんない in speech. Fine spoken, never written in anything formal.
すみません to a close friend sounds stiff, or sarcastic. Friends get ごめん or ごめんね.
そうですね often just buys time; そうだね agrees. If you actually need thinking time casually, stretch it: そうだなあ.
も drops as well. 食べてもいい？ is also fine and slightly more careful.
に drops, and の makes you sound interested rather than demanding. Bare どこ行く？ works but lands blunter.

items.polite: 明日、お時間ありますか。
items.note: 暇 is the normal casual word for free time, but never upward: 暇ですか？ to a boss implies they have nothing to do.

items.polite: ありがとうございます。
items.note: あざす, a crushed ありがとうございます, exists but belongs to young men and part-time staff. Out of the right mouth it sounds like bad acting.

modules.title: Contractions 縮約形
modules.blurb: The forms you learned, squeezed the way people actually pronounce them. Half of listening comprehension is just recognising these.
modules.note: None of these are wrong or lazy — they are the normal spoken pronunciations. What matters is that most of them do not belong in writing, so learn both directions: produce the left column on paper, the right column out loud.

items.note: The い just drops. This one even survives into polite speech: 食べてます is normal in almost any conversation.
〜ているの → 〜てんの (and を drops on the way). The る before の collapses to ん everywhere: やってるの→やってんの, 言ってるの→言ってんの.
〜ておく→〜とく, 〜でおく→〜どく. 買っておく→買っとく, やっておく→やっとく.
〜てしまう→〜ちゃう. It carries either 'completely' or 'oops' — here, clearly oops.
After the voiced て-forms it is 〜でしまう→〜じゃう: 読んじゃう, 死んじゃう.
Usually the sentence stops right there, with いけない left unsaid. Finishing it (行かなきゃいけない) sounds more deliberate.
〜なくては→〜なくちゃ. Interchangeable with なきゃ; なくちゃ feels slightly softer and a touch more feminine, but only slightly.
ら→ん before ない. Same with つまらない→つまんない, 変わらない→変わんない, 信じられない→信じらんない.
ではない→じゃない is so complete that ではない now reads as written or oratorical, not merely polite.
ら抜き言葉. Standard in speech across every age group now, and still marked wrong in writing and by some older people. Note it makes 'can eat' and 'is eaten' distinguishable, which is why it won.
〜ai crushes to 〜ee: うまい→うめえ, やばい→やべえ, 高い→たけえ. Rough and strongly male. Women use it, but usually for comic effect.
Opens a sentence that redirects what was just said. てゆーか and つーか are the same word; てか is the shortest and most common in texts.
The same squeeze keeps going: それでは→それじゃ→じゃあ→じゃ. All four are alive, in descending order of formality.
Spelled ほんとう, said ほんと by nearly everyone. ほんっとに with the small っ is the emphatic version.
すいません is how most people actually pronounce it. Perfectly normal spoken, but write すみません.

modules.title: Spoken shapes 話し言葉
modules.blurb: じゃん, っす, って, trailing けど — the little structures that carry casual conversation and that textbooks skip.

items.note: じゃん is じゃない used to push agreement — you are telling someone what they should already think. It comes out of the Tōkai and Kōshin regions and spread nationally through Yokohama; young speakers everywhere use it now. Never aim it upward.
The complaint flavour of じゃん — a mild accusation. Fine with friends, genuinely rude to a 先輩.

っす is です crushed flat: respectful in intention, relaxed in sound. It is heavily male and belongs to sports clubs, kitchens, trades and young office juniors talking to a 先輩 they are comfortable with. Women rarely use it, and in a formal company it reads as sloppy. Never to a client or a teacher.

items.r: たなか、きょうこないって。
items.en: Tanaka says he's not coming today.
items.note: って is the casual と言っていた, with the source placed in front. It is how almost all secondhand information gets reported in speech.

items.en: What's that thing you just mentioned?
items.note: って also replaces は as a topic marker, and it points specifically at something just said. それは何？ is a neutral question; それって何？ picks up their words.

items.ja: 明日でもいいんだけど。
items.r: あしたでもいいんだけど。
items.en: Tomorrow would work for me too, if that's alright…
items.note: A sentence left hanging on けど is not unfinished — the trailing けど is the softener. Completing the thought would make it pushy.

items.ja: 疲れてるし、今日はやめとく。
items.r: つかれてるし、きょうはやめとく。
items.en: I'm tired, so I'll skip today.
items.note: し gives one reason while hinting there are others you are not listing. Gentler than から, which sounds like you are arguing a case.
の asks for an explanation and sounds concerned. どうした？ without it is blunter and reads as masculine.
な appears before んだ after nouns and な-adjectives — 休みなんだ, 静かなんだ — but not after verbs or い-adjectives: 行くんだ, 忙しいんだ.

items.ja: なんか、うまく言えないんだけどさ。
items.r: なんか、うまくいえないんだけどさ。
items.en: I dunno, I can't put it well, but…
items.note: なんか is the spoken 'like' or 'sort of'. It buys a beat and hedges what follows. One per sentence is natural; three makes you sound scattered, exactly as in English.

modules.title: Sentence-final particles 終助詞
modules.blurb: The layer that carries how you feel. Get these wrong and grammatically perfect Japanese still sounds cold or bossy.

items.en: There's a test tomorrow, you know.
items.note: よ delivers information the listener does not have. Attached to a bare command (早くしろよ) it turns pushy, but on a statement it is neutral for everyone.
ね checks that you are both in the same place emotionally. Constant よ with no ね is the clearest marker of a non-native speaker — it makes you sound like you are lecturing.
よね asserts and checks at once: 'I'm telling you this, and you agree, right?' The most useful particle combination in the language.
な is ね turned inward — you are saying it to yourself, out loud, and anyone may do that. Aimed at another person it hardens: 早くしろよな is rough and male, and 行くな is a different な entirely ('don't go').
Stretching to なあ buys thinking time and is completely safe for any speaker. Its polite twin is そうですねえ.

Textbooks call わ feminine. That is the rising Tokyo-drama わ (そうだわ), which now sounds dated or theatrical from anyone under fifty. The flat, falling わ — 知らんわ, 疲れたわ, しんどいわ — is ordinary casual speech: male-leaning in Tokyo, used by everyone in Kansai. Same character, two unrelated particles.

ぞ is real, but mostly self-directed psyching-up rather than something you aim at a person, and it is male-leaning. ぜ (行くぜ) is far rarer off-screen than on it — used to someone's face it sounds like you are doing a voice.
かな wonders out loud; かなあ wonders longer. It is also the softest way to ask a favour: 手伝ってくれるかな — 'any chance you'd help?'

items.r: あしたってやすみだっけ？
items.en: Tomorrow's a day off — right? I've forgotten.
items.note: っけ marks something you once knew and have mislaid. Fine about dates and plans; used about a person's name to their face (名前、何だっけ？) it stings.

items.ja: 昨日さ、駅で田中に会ってさ。
items.r: きのうさ、えきでたなかにあってさ。
items.en: So yesterday, right, I ran into Tanaka at the station…
items.note: さ chops a story into beats and holds the floor while you tell it. Common in Tokyo speech from all genders; stacked too thickly it reads as young or pushy.

modules.title: Listening noises 相槌
modules.blurb: Japanese listening is loud. Going quiet while someone talks does not read as polite attention — it reads as boredom or disagreement.

items.note: Say it every few seconds, far more often than you would say 'uh-huh' in English. The polite equivalent is はい, used identically — on the phone people say はい almost continuously, and silence makes the other person stop and ask if you are still there.
The workhorse response to new information. Falling tone means 'I hear you'; rising そうなんだ？ means mild surprise. Polite version: そうなんですね.
Genuine mild surprise. Short and flat (へえ。) reads as bored — the stretch is what makes it friendly.
Specifically confirms that the other person has correctly guessed or restated what you meant. Not a general 'yes'.
Concedes the point without committing to full agreement. Extremely common among adults and the safest thing to say about an opinion you do not actually share.

Signals you have followed a reason or explanation. It is mildly evaluative, so upward it can sound like you are grading your boss — and なるほどですね is a famous piece of bad business Japanese. Use おっしゃる通りです or 勉強になります instead.
Not 'I understand' but 'I have felt exactly that'. The stretched vowel is doing the empathy; flat わかる。 sounds like a factual claim.

The everyday surprise reaction, used by all genders and well past thirty among friends. Casual only — never to a boss, a client or a teacher. まじ？ alone is blunter; 本当に？ is the version that is safe everywhere.
Aimed more at yourself than at the other person, usually on hearing something bad. Male-leaning but widely used.

Originally 'dangerous', now a pure intensity marker that can be positive or negative: やばい、おいしい (incredible) and やばい、遅刻する (I'm screwed) are both normal. Tone carries the entire meaning. Fine between friends of any gender; at work it marks you as young and unpolished. やば。 is the clipped form, やべえ the rough male one.
Strong agreement, and firmly young — roughly teens through twenties. Older speakers do use it, but usually knowingly; said straight past about thirty it can sound like you are reaching.
Sympathy is expected out loud and promptly. Letting someone's bad news sit without a reaction is read as indifference, not as giving them space.

modules.title: Turning down a friend 断り方
modules.blurb: A flat 行かない ends the invitation and dents the friendship. The casual refusal has the same shape as the business one — react, reason, offer an alternative, close warmly.

options: 誘ってくれてありがとう！
あー、めっちゃ行きたい！
slots.note: React to the invitation before you refuse it. Leading with your reason makes the refusal about your calendar instead of about them, which is what stings.

options: でもその日、用事があって。
でもちょっと今週きつくて。
その日バイトなんだよね。
slots.note: Vague is normal and expected. 用事があって covers anything. Over-explaining is what makes an excuse sound invented.

options: 来週ならいつでも空いてるよ。
slots.note: This part is not decoration. Without an alternative, a Japanese friend may read the refusal as 'stop asking me' and quietly stop asking.
楽しんできてね sends them off warmly and is the most natural close when you are not coming. The stretched 〜 is tone of voice; without it the line reads clipped.

cushions.en: Ah, that's a bit… — the refusal everyone understands without you finishing it
I'll come if I can — widely understood, especially in Kansai, as a polite no
our schedules just don't line up

cushions.ja: 気持ちだけもらっとくね
cushions.r: きもちだけもらっとくね
cushions.en: I'll take the thought, if not the thing — for turning down a gift or a favour

modules.title: Texting 文字のやりとり
modules.blurb: LINE Japanese is its own dialect: shorter, warmer, and full of marks that exist only in writing.

items.note: Perfect to a friend. Sent upward at work it is considered curt — reply 承知しました to a boss or client. 了解です softens it, but not enough for everyone. Teens shorten it all the way to just り.
Clipped お疲れ様. Fine to friends and club mates; write お疲れ様です in full to anyone senior.

The three ways to laugh in writing. w comes from 笑い: one w is a token chuckle, www is real laughter. 笑 tacked on the end (なにそれ笑) is the softer, all-ages version. 草 began as a joke about wwww looking like a row of grass and is now a word in its own right, said out loud as well as typed: 草, or 草生える. None of them go anywhere near a work email.

items.ja: ごめん、今電車。あとで連絡する！
items.r: ごめん、いまでんしゃ。あとでれんらくする！
items.en: Sorry, on the train — I'll message you later!
items.note: Texts drop verbs wholesale. 今電車 is 今電車に乗っている with everything predictable removed.
集合 is the ordinary word for meeting up at a set time and place. It looks stiff on the page but is completely casual in use.

items.en: leaving a message read and unanswered
items.note: LINE shows the sender the moment you open their message, so silence is visible in a way it is not elsewhere. 既読スルー is a real small injury between friends; a one-character おけ costs nothing.
OK → おけ, and in typed form おk (the K never converted). Harmless and friendly among people your own age; with the age gap wrong it dates you instantly in either direction.

items.ja: 返事遅くなってごめん！
items.r: へんじおそくなってごめん！
items.note: Expected after a day or so of silence, even between close friends. The polite version is 返信が遅くなり申し訳ありません.
From なるべく早く, and common in casual work chat too. Related clips: とりま (from とりあえず、まあ — 'for now'), ワンチャン ('there's a chance that…'), ガチ ('for real', as in ガチで面白い).

The 〜 is tone of voice in writing: it lengthens the vowel and warms up anything. A bare ありがとう。 in a text, with a full stop, can read as cold — which is why Japanese texts so often have no full stops at all.
